extracted.intended_audience: small businesses, employers, in-house/outside counsel, HR professionals, SBA and other stakeholders participating in FTC rulemaking on non-competes
extracted.subtask_description: Regulatory guidance and agency responses addressing comments from small businesses about the FTC's final rule banning non-compete clauses, including compliance requirements, estimated costs, exceptions, and evidentiary expectations for asserted harms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggregate competitive effects of non-competes
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission finds, based on expertise, empirical evidence, and the record, that non-competes tend to negatively affect competitive conditions in labor and product and service markets, including by inhibiting new business formation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission focuses on aggregate effects across firms (including small businesses) rather than isolated cases where an individual small business may benefit; aggregate harms justify the final rule even if some individual firms benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for empirical support for claims of small-business harm
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments asserting that banning non-competes would cause small business closures or other harms must be supported by empirical research or evidence; the Commission found no empirical research correlating decreased non-compete enforceability with firm closures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absent evidence, the Commission will not assume causation; anecdotal claims are weighed against available empirical studies showing aggregate effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability of less-restrictive alternatives to protect confidential information
rubrics_metrics.description: Businesses, including small businesses, have sufficient, less restrictive alternatives such as NDAs, trade secrets law, fixed-term contracts, worker retention policies, and maintaining security of confidential information to protect trade secrets and proprietary information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These alternatives are considered accessible to small businesses and can largely substitute for non-competes without the anticompetitive harms of non-competes; the Commission references Part IV.D for detailed discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on entering new non-competes
rubrics_metrics.description: It is an unfair method of competition to enter into a non-compete with a worker after the effective date; small entities can no longer enter into new non-competes with incoming workers, including senior executives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compliance may include revising HR materials, manuals, templates, and making strategic employment-term decisions; this may entail one-time legal or HR effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction on enforcing existing non-competes (except senior executives)
rubrics_metrics.description: Small entities cannot enforce (or make misrepresentations about enforcement of) existing non-competes for workers other than senior executives after the effective date; businesses must refrain from suing or threatening to sue such workers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal contract rescission is not required. Employers must provide notice to affected workers (safe harbor model language provided) but only to workers with known contact information; see §910.2(b) notice requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exception permitting existing senior executive non-competes
rubrics_metrics.description: Existing non-competes with senior executives are allowed to remain in force under the final rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission found senior executive non-competes are most likely to have involved consideration and thus permitted them to continue; employers should identify senior executives whose non-competes are unaffected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarified definition of 'non-compete clause' to reduce evasion
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule provides greater clarity on the definition of a non-compete clause (described in Part III.D) to reduce confusion and evasion, and to determine which terms meet the definition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This clarification is intended to limit use of borderline de facto non-competes and aid enforcement; related restrictive terms remain subject to antitrust law if they are anticompetitive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-solicitation and TRAPs treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule does not ban non-solicitation clauses or TRAPs unless they meet the definition of a non-compete clause; the rule also does not prohibit agreements preventing a worker from working for two firms simultaneously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commission weighs marginal benefits of non-solicitation clauses against harms from non-competes and found those marginal benefits insufficient to justify non-competes; firms may still use non-solicitation clauses that do not qualify as non-competes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elimination of the 25% sale-of-business threshold
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission is eliminating the proposed 25% threshold for the sale-of-business exception, allowing more small-business owners to utilize non-competes for owners when selling their business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While individual businesses might see decreased sale value, the Commission justifies the change based on net aggregate benefits of freeing labor and product markets from non-competes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adherence to SBA definition of 'small business' and rejection of categorical small-business exception
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission declines to create a small business exception and follows the SBA definition of 'small business' per 13 CFR 121.201; agencies cannot deviate from this definition without procedures in 13 CFR 121.903.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No empirical evidence supports a categorical small business exception; commenters requesting different definitions (e.g., employee-count based) were considered but rejected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employer notice requirement and safe-harbor procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers must provide notice to workers (other than senior executives) that their non-compete will not be enforced; §910.2(b)(4) includes model language constituting notice, and §910.2(b)(5) provides a safe harbor for compliance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notice is required only to workers with known contact information; the Commission estimates digital notices take 20 minutes of an HR specialist's time and provides per-notice cost assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on misrepresentations about enforceability
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers cannot enforce non-competes for non-senior-executive workers after the effective date, and they may not make misrepresentations about their enforceability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is part of the unfair methods of competition prohibitions in §910.2(a)(1)(ii) and (iii); employers must adjust communications and contract language accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: One-time (non-recurring) compliance design
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule is designed to require only a one-time action by employers and imposes no recurring compliance requirements to minimize ongoing burdens for small employers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This design consideration impacts the Commission's cost-benefit assessment and the IRFA conclusions about burdens on small firms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimated legal cost assumptions for compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: To ensure incoming workers' contracts do not include non-competes, the Commission assumes one hour of a lawyer's time per firm valued at $134.62; updating contractual practices is assumed to average 4–8 hours of lawyer time per firm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These assumptions produce per-firm cost estimates ($538.48–$1,076.96 for updating contractual practices) and aggregate national estimates; the Commission notes heterogeneity and that these are conservative/average assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimated administrative cost assumptions for notification
rubrics_metrics.description: Composing and sending digital notice is estimated to take 20 minutes of an HR specialist (median wage $31.85/hr) costing $21.23 per establishment; mailed notice per worker is estimated at $1.81 (printing, postage, one minute HR time).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission uses these assumptions to estimate total direct compliance costs (e.g., $57.5 million for digital notices to establishments and $1.1 million for mailed notices), with conservative assumptions that each establishment sends its own communications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation that many firms already use overlapping restrictive covenants
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence indicates that large shares of workers with non-competes are also subject to NDAs, non-solicitation, or non-recruitment agreements (e.g., statistics from Balasubramanian et al.), so many firms may not need to expand other restrictive covenants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This finding informs the Commission's assessment that some firms will opt to make no contractual changes and that average update cost estimates incorporate heterogeneity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pecuniary benefits do not justify anticompetitive practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Pecuniary benefits to a firm engaged in an anticompetitive practice (e.g., reduced litigation costs or retention advantages from non-competes) are not a cognizable defense for an anticompetitive practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commission rejects arguments that firm-level financial benefits outweigh the aggregate harms to competition when assessing justification for non-competes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of ban on litigation dynamics and leveling the playing field
rubrics_metrics.description: A bright-line ban on non-competes will reduce non-compete litigation and the associated dynamics where large firms can drive up litigation costs to disadvantage smaller firms; the ban could better level the playing field for small firms seeking talent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commission notes no evidence that trade-secret litigation will increase following bans and that the litigation threat already exists under current non-compete enforcement patterns.
